The test image shows a tomato plant pulled from soil with:
- Stem split open near the soil line revealing brown/yellow vascular tissue
- White cottony mycelium on the stem exterior at soil level
- Dead/wilted leaves and brown roots
- Sandy soil

Key candidates: Southern_Blight (white mycelium at soil line), Sclerotinia_Timber_Rot, Verticillium_Wilt, Bacterial_Wilt. Let me view reference images one per class.
The Southern Blight Bugwood_23 shows white mycelium with sclerotia on the stem — very similar to the test image. Let me check more classes.

I've now viewed all 16 reference images across 16 classes. Here is my analysis:

**Test image key features:**
- Stem pulled from sandy soil, split open at the soil line
- White cottony mycelial material coating the stem exterior at soil level
- Internal vascular tissue is yellow-brown (discolored)
- Plant completely dead, leaves dry/brown

**Reference comparison:**
- **Southern_Blight/Bugwood_23**: Closest match — shows white/gray mycelium with tiny sclerotia coating the stem, same presentation site (stem base). The sandy soil in field views (Bugwood_5, 1568116) also matches.
- **Sclerotinia_Timber_Rot**: White mycelium present but with large black sclerotia; typically affects aerial stems, not soil-line stem base.
- **Bacterial_Wilt / Southern_Bacterial_Wilt**: Both show bacterial streaming test; no external mycelium.
- **Verticillium_Wilt**: Shows internal vascular browning but no white exterior mycelium.
- All leaf disease classes (Early Blight, Septoria, Powdery Mildew, etc.) are clearly not matching.

**Decision**: The white mycelium at the soil line + stem base rot + sandy soil + plant collapse is the hallmark presentation of Southern Blight (*Sclerotium rolfsii*). The Bugwood_23 reference (1568068 vs 1575274) is the closest visual match.
